strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and important problem—safety alignment of Video LLMs—with a large-scale, real-world benchmark (VideoSafetyEval) spanning 19 subcategories, 6 principal risk categories, and 10 languages, substantially larger in scale than prior image-safety benchmarks (SIUO, SPA-VL, FigStep, VLGuard, MMBench, SafeBench).

Extensive empirical evaluation of 21 mainstream Video LLMs reveals a clear and interesting finding: integrating video modality substantially degrades safety performance (avg. 34.2% DSR drop) relative to text-only inputs, with controlled ablations (FPS, frame count, semantic harmfulness, video length) that help disentangle causes of this vulnerability.

Proposed defense framework VideoSafety-R1 (VST dataset + AT-SFT + Safety-guided GRPO) yields large, consistent safety gains across multiple video and image safety benchmarks (VSE-HH, MMBench, VLGuard, FigStep) while only modestly affecting general video understanding capability, and outperforms several strong image-domain defense baselines (SPA-VL, MM-RLHF, Self-Reminder, VLGuard).

Very thorough appendix: dataset-quality verification via human annotation agreement (query/video label accuracy, analysis reliability), validation of the LLM-judge (Qwen-Long) against human labels and other frontier LLM judges, computational cost/latency analysis, cross-lingual analysis, attention-sink mechanistic analysis, and abundant qualitative case studies improve transparency and (partial) reproducibility.
Thoughtful ethics/reproducibility statement covering dataset access control, PII blurring, sensitive-word bias checking, and code release.
weaknesses: The entire evaluation pipeline (DSR, Helpfulness Score) relies on a single commercial LLM judge (Qwen-Long), and the training data (captions, harmfulness labels, CoT annotations) is generated largely by other Qwen-family models (Qwen-Max-VL, Qwen-Long). This creates a risk of circularity/family bias between the models used to construct training supervision and the model used to judge success, which is not fully addressed despite the reliability study in Appendix J.3.

Data construction (captioning, harmfulness classification, query generation, CoT generation) is almost entirely LLM-driven with only partial human spot-checks (1,000/10,000 samples), leaving open the possibility that systematic labeling biases or errors propagate through both the benchmark and the training/RL reward signals.

The false refusal rate (FRR) increases notably for VideoLLaMA3-2B+VideoSafety-R1 (+12.7%), which is a meaningful helpfulness/safety trade-off that is somewhat downplayed as 'acceptable' rather than critically analyzed.

Core technical contributions (alarm tokens as auxiliary classification heads, GRPO with rule-based dual-modality reward, dynamic reward adaptation) are largely recombinations of existing techniques (GRPO, attention-sink analysis, classifier-guided fine-tuning) rather than fundamentally new mechanisms, making the technical novelty moderate.

Case studies show fairly templated, repetitive refusal/justification language across different harm categories, consistent with the paper's own admission that CoT reasoning data (generated via fixed prompt templates and Qwen-Max) may lack naturalness/diversity — this raises concern about how much of the improvement reflects genuine safety reasoning versus template-matching optimized for the same-family judge.

Comparison baselines (SPA-VL, MM-RLHF, VLGuard, Self-Reminder) are only applied to Qwen2.5-VL-7B and trained with different data scales/recipes than VideoSafety-R1, making some head-to-head comparisons less controlled.

The claim that 'video modality degrades safety' is partly based on comparing full video input vs. text-only (no-vision) input, which are qualitatively different tasks (the model may simply default to refusal without visual context); the framing could be more nuanced regarding what portion of the drop is attributable to genuine unsafe multimodal reasoning versus lack of contextual grounding.
